tasks.short: Gather usage figures and requests, confer with colleagues and faculty on collection and services, plan programmes with community organisations, arrange dates and rooms, and write up decisions.

steps.what: Librarian gathers usage figures and requests before the meeting
Librarian confers with colleagues and faculty to make collection decisions and determine library services
Librarian confers with community organisations to plan informational programs
Librarian arranges dates and rooms with partners by e-mail
Librarian writes up decisions and actions

tasks.design: A usage dashboard in the library system ({OTHER}) shows loans, holds and purchase requests per subject, so figures are not compiled by hand. A shared room calendar shows free slots when dates are agreed with partners, and the librarian writes decisions into a short template in the document space ({DOCS}). Conferring with colleagues, faculty and community organisations stays with the librarian.
tasks.previous_blocker: Figures were exported to spreadsheets, and dates agreed in long e-mail threads.
tasks.enabler_now: Library systems include usage dashboards; shared calendars show room availability.
tasks.still_hard: Community partners have their own calendars and priorities.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which partner will actually bring people to a programme.

reach.learn: Whether shared figures make collection meetings shorter.

evidence.claim: Library systems offer usage dashboards with loans, holds and requests.
No Annex III high-risk area applies to library collection work.

assumptions: Boundary: from loan data to decision notes; running the programmes is outside.
Input contract: loan and request data from the library system; room calendar kept by facilities; fallback is spreadsheets and e-mail.

Conferring keeps its full time. s4 keeps 70: the room calendar ends checking rooms with facilities, but agreeing dates with partners stays. s5 keeps 90: the template gives headings, but writing decisions and actions is a first record.
research_questions: Do collection decisions use more current figures?

already_counted.description: Librarian reads the usage dashboard before meetings.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many requests still come by mail and are counted by hand (s1 70) (9.5); high: loans, holds and requests are all in the dashboard (14.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Read book reviews, publisher catalogs and faculty recommendations, check holdings and loans, select titles within budget, send orders and update the budget.

steps.what: Librarian reads book reviews, publisher catalogs and faculty recommendations
Librarian checks current holdings and loans for each title
Librarian evaluates materials and selects titles within the budget
Librarian types orders on the supplier's order form: by hand today; after the change the module builds the electronic order from the selection
Librarian checks the order before it goes: titles, editions, quantities, prices, supplier and fund match the selection
Librarian releases the checked electronic order to the supplier
Librarian updates the budget spreadsheet with the ordered amounts: by hand today; after the change the module commits the released order's amounts to the fund

tasks.design: The acquisitions module of the library system ({OTHER}) collects new-title feeds from suppliers and faculty requests in one list, marks titles already held with their loan counts, and shows the remaining budget per fund. The librarian evaluates and selects; the module builds an electronic order from the selection, the librarian checks it and releases it once to the supplier, and the module commits the released amounts to the fund.
tasks.previous_blocker: Catalogues, requests and holdings were checked in separate places, and orders and budgets typed by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Acquisitions modules take supplier feeds, check holdings and send electronic orders.
tasks.still_hard: Small and foreign publishers are outside the feeds.
tasks.human_edge: Choosing the title the collection lacks rather than the one everyone reviews.
tasks.altitude: The librarian selects from one list instead of assembling it.

reach.learn: Whether requests in the module get answered sooner.

evidence.claim: Library acquisitions modules take supplier title feeds, check holdings and send electronic orders.
Basic business records are kept for 7 years and must stay usable at an audit.

assumptions: Boundary: from catalogues and requests to the committed budget; receiving books is outside.
Input contract: title feeds from main suppliers; faculty requests through the module's form; fund budgets set by the library director; fallback is catalogues and spreadsheets.

Evaluating and selecting keep their full time. The fund commitment is the module's own record of the released order in the same system, so it has no separate approval; it carries the amounts checked in s4a.
Faculty use the request form as they now send e-mails; about the same time.

already_counted.description: Librarian reviews the merged title list.

incremental.description: Librarian keeps supplier feeds and fund codes current.

approvals.approved_version: The electronic order with titles, editions, quantities, prices and fund exactly as checked by the librarian in s4a, sent once to the named supplier from the acquisitions module; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many titles come from small or foreign publishers outside the feeds, so reading, holdings checks and order typing stay partly by hand (s1 80, s2 50, s4 50) (28.5); high: most titles come from main suppliers (45.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Collect usage statistics per package, evaluate vendor performance, negotiate contracts, check the final text, get the director's signature, return the contract and place orders.

steps.what: Librarian collects usage statistics per database and journal package
Librarian evaluates vendor products and performance on access, delivery and service
Librarian negotiates contracts and prices with vendors
Librarian checks the final contract text against the agreed terms
Library director approves and signs the contract
Librarian posts the signed contract back to the vendor
Librarian prepares orders under the new contract: by e-mail today; in the acquisitions module with the contract's packages and prices after the change
Librarian checks each order before it goes: packages, prices and period match the signed contract and the vendor is right
Librarian releases the checked orders to the vendor

tasks.design: Standard usage reports are harvested from vendors automatically into a cost-per-use dashboard ({BI}), and delivery delays and access outages come from the acquisitions module. Negotiating stays with the librarian. The librarian checks the final text, the director signs on the e-signature platform ({ESIGN}), which returns the contract, and orders under it are prepared in the acquisitions module, checked by the librarian and released once.
tasks.previous_blocker: Usage reports were downloaded per vendor and combined in spreadsheets; contracts went by post.
tasks.enabler_now: Vendors publish standard usage reports that can be harvested automatically.
tasks.still_hard: Big publishers set terms the library can barely move.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which cancellation threat a vendor will take seriously.
tasks.altitude: The librarian negotiates from a ready dashboard instead of building it.

evidence.claim: Library vendors publish standard usage reports that can be harvested automatically.
Basic business records, including contracts, are kept for 7 years.

assumptions: Boundary: from usage reports to orders placed; paying invoices is outside.
Input contract: usage reports from vendors in the standard format; delivery data from the acquisitions module; fallback is manual downloads.
Negotiating and checking do not change.
The director's signing time is outside the librarian's savings.
Coverage for s1: about 75% of database and journal packages deliver standard usage reports that the {BI} connector harvests each month; the rest are downloaded by hand, so s1 keeps 40%.
research_questions: Do cancellations follow cost per use more closely?

approvals.approved_version: The contract text exactly as checked by the librarian in s4 and signed by the library director in s5, returned once to the vendor through the e-signature platform; any change needs a new check and signature.

The orders with packages, prices and period exactly as checked by the librarian in s7b against the signed contract, sent once to that vendor from the acquisitions module; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: only about half of packages deliver standard reports, so more are downloaded by hand (s1 70) (20.7); high: about 75% are harvested as assumed (28.3).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Plan who does what each week, show staff how to receive, shelve and catalogue, answer their questions, check new staff's catalogue records and keep training checklists.

steps.what: Librarian plans who does what each week on paper
Librarian trains library staff in receiving, shelving, researching and cataloging
Librarian answers staff questions during the work
Librarian checks new staff's catalogue records
Librarian keeps a training checklist per staff member

tasks.design: The week plan sits in a shared staff schedule, and how-to pages for receiving, shelving and cataloguing in the staff wiki ({DOCS}) answer routine questions so the librarian takes fewer of them. Catalogue records are checked by code against the shared catalogue rules, so the librarian reviews flagged records and reads a sample of unflagged ones for meaning. Training checklists move to the learning system ({LMS}). Training staff stays in person; flags count records, not people's speed.
tasks.previous_blocker: Plans were on paper, every question came to the librarian, and every new record was checked by eye.
tasks.enabler_now: Library systems validate records against catalogue rules; staff wikis hold how-to pages.
tasks.still_hard: New staff still need someone beside them for the first weeks.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing which new colleague needs encouragement rather than correction.

evidence.claim: Library systems validate catalogue records against shared catalogue rules and flag errors.
Works council consent is needed if system logs check a cataloguer's output.

assumptions: Boundary: from staff availability to training checklists; hiring is outside.
Input contract: availability from the staff schedule; catalogue rules from the shared catalogue; fallback is paper and checking by eye.

Training in person keeps its full time. s1 keeps 80: availability sits next to the plan and the plan is not copied out, but deciding who does what stays. s4 keeps 70: code catches rule breaks, but the librarian still reads flagged records and a sample of others to check that subject and classification fit the item. s5 keeps 80: the learning system lists the standard items per role, but ticking off training stays a first record.
Record flags are not used to rate staff.
research_questions: Do new staff reach full speed sooner?

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: staff still ask most questions in person and the rules catch few errors (s3 95, s4 85) (8.2); high: the wiki answers routine questions and flags work as assumed (13.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The librarian keeps conferring, selecting, negotiating and training; compiling figures, typing orders, downloading reports and checking every record shrink.
role.ambitious_version: A librarian who spends saved time with users and partners.
